messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Software Engineer
- Trauma Type: Refugee
- Pcl5: 44

He is 77, a married African man who has spent much of his life trying to stay useful, steady, and invisible in the ways that matter. Even now, as a software engineer, he keeps a disciplined routine. He likes problems with clear logic, lines of code that can be traced, errors that can be found and fixed. For years, that kind of order has helped him hold together experiences that never felt orderly at all.

He first learns what it means to be a refugee as a younger man, when the life he knows is torn apart by violence and sudden threat. He does not describe the event first; he circles around it, as if approaching a place in the mind that still feels dangerous. What he remembers most clearly is the confusion that follows. There are people running, shouting, carrying what they can. There is the urgent decision to leave, not because he wants to, but because staying means death or disappearance. He and his family move with crowds of others, moving between fear and exhaustion, each day defined by finding water, shelter, or a place where the children can sleep without crying too loudly. He learns quickly that in displacement, privacy disappears. Hunger, humiliation, and uncertainty become normal. He becomes careful with his face and voice, always watching for signs that something worse is about to happen.

What stays with him most is not one image alone but the sense of being stripped of control. In the years that follow, even after he reaches safety, his body does not fully accept that the danger is over. He sleeps lightly and wakes often, especially when there is a noise outside the house or a sudden knock at the door. At night, his mind returns to old routes, old faces, old moments of waiting. He has dreams in which he is back in flight, unable to gather his family quickly enough. Sometimes he wakes with his heart pounding and needs several minutes before he can orient himself to the room around him. His wife has learned to speak to him gently when he startles, because sharp words or sudden movement can make him visibly tense, as if he is bracing for impact.

He builds a new life through work, and software engineering gives him a structure he can trust. Computers behave according to rules, even when people do not. He can concentrate for long stretches and take pride in making things function again. But he notices that his attention is not as steady as it once was. When he is under pressure, he becomes impatient and irritable, especially if there are interruptions. He double-checks doors, windows, and calendars in ways that can seem excessive to others, but to him it feels like necessary vigilance. He dislikes crowded places and chooses seats with his back to the wall. If someone speaks loudly behind him, his shoulders tighten before he can stop them.

Over time, he notices that he is often on guard without meaning to be. He scans faces, listens for changes in tone, and reads ordinary situations for hidden danger. This vigilance has helped him survive, but it has also narrowed his world. He avoids conversations about conflict, and when news reports show refugees, war, or mass displacement, he turns away or leaves the room. He tells himself he is too old to be haunted by the past, yet the old memories still arrive with a force that surprises him. At times he feels a wave of sadness for the life interrupted, for the opportunities lost, for the years spent carrying fear in silence.

His marriage has become one of the few places where he allows himself to be less guarded. His wife knows that he can become distant when overwhelmed. She sees the small signs: the long silences, the stiffness in his posture, the way he stops speaking when a memory has caught hold of him. He is not an easy man to draw out, but he values her steadiness and the ordinary rituals they have built together. He continues to work, though he is aware that the effort of keeping his thoughts organized takes more energy than before. He feels old in a way that is not just about age. It is the weight of having lived through loss that never fully resolves, the persistence of a body that still reacts as if danger might return at any moment.
